instructions: Place parsnips, cream, and water in a saucepot. Add additional water as needed to cover the parsnips.
Bring to a simmer and cook until parsnips have no resistance to a paring knife.
Transfer parsnips and thickened liquid to a blender. Start low, then gradually increase speed.
With blender running, add butter and a conservative pinch of salt. Process until extremely smooth.
Check seasoning and consistency; adjust with salt and/or additional water to preference.
recipes.notes: Unlike potato purée: parsnips are cooked in the cream itself. Technique transfers to rutabaga, carrot, celeriac, and sunchokes.

recipes.name: Eggplant & Garlic Confit
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Remove tops and bottoms of eggplants, cut in half lengthwise.
Score flesh in a crosshatch pattern and lightly salt to draw out moisture and bitterness. Rest flesh-side down on a paper-towel–lined sheet pan for 25 minutes.
Lay eggplants flesh-side down in a baking dish. Add garlic and bouquet garni.
Heat oil to 250°F and carefully ladle it over the eggplants. If they float, weight them with a wire cake rack to keep submerged.
Bake in a 300°F oven, check for tenderness after 45 minutes. Ideal texture is creamy with no resistance.
To serve immediately: drain on paper towels, arrange with confit garlic, drizzle with balsamic, finish with oregano and Maldon.
To store: keep eggplant submerged in oil in an airtight container in the fridge up to 1 week.
recipes.notes: Leftover oil is great in vinaigrettes or sautéing — hasn't reached its smoke point. Try the smashed-garlic-on-toast move for a snack.

recipes.name: Pan-Roasted Zucchini with Vierge Sauce
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Pan-roast zucchini in olive oil until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add herbs or garlic and immediately remove from heat to prevent burning.
Spoon vierge sauce (warm olive oil + tomato concassé + lemon + herbs) over plated zucchini.
recipes.notes: Workbook ingredient list is partial — flesh out with standard ratios when cooking. Vierge sauce pairs broadly with vegetables and fish.

recipes.name: Baked Beets
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I

ingredients.name: red beets, leaves and stems removed

instructions: Wash and dry trimmed beets. Place on aluminum foil, shiny side up. Drizzle with oil and season with kosher salt.
Fold foil into a pouch and place in a baking dish, folded side up.
Bake at 350°F for ~45 minutes. Test with a paring knife for no resistance.
Peel while still warm under running water or with gloves over parchment (beets stain).
Cut into wedges or preferred shape.
In a mixing bowl, combine beets, minced shallot, Maldon, balsamic, EVOO, and most of the chives. Reserve a sprinkle of chives for garnish.
Spoon dressed beets into a serving bowl and finish with the reserved chives.
recipes.notes: Use true balsamic (DOP-certified Modena/Emilia-Romagna). Season while warm so beets absorb the marinade. Technique works for golden and Chioggia beets — vary the vinegar.

recipes.name: Mayonnaise
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Separate yolk from white and remove the chalazae (white string).
Wrap a damp twisted kitchen towel around the base of the mixing bowl to stabilize.
Whisk the yolk; add Dijon (flavor + emulsifier).
Whisking continuously, slowly drizzle in oil. As mayo thickens, add small amounts of water, vinegar, and lemon juice (strain lemon for seeds).
If it breaks: add more Dijon to re-emulsify.
Whisking speed can increase as the emulsion volume grows.
Stop adding oil at the desired viscosity (peaks form) and quantity. Finish with salt and acid to taste. Store in a glass jar in the fridge.
recipes.notes: The building block for aiolis, remoulades, dressings, and sauces. McGee's principle: a yolk absorbs near-infinite fat as long as moisture stays balanced.

recipes.name: Remoulade
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I

ingredients.name: fines herbes (parsley, chives, tarragon — equal parts, minced)

instructions: Starting with 400 g mayonnaise, add capers, cornichons, fines herbes, shallots, and salt.
Stir with a rubber spatula to combine.
Capers are salty — taste before adding the full salt amount.
recipes.notes: Keller: would rather you skip the recipe than use dried herbs. Serve as a side sauce with fish or roast chicken.

recipes.name: Hollandaise
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Quick clarified butter: seal butter in a heavy-duty bag, set in simmering water in a stockpot until melted. Transfer to fridge with one corner of the bag at the lowest position. Once solidified, snip the bottom corner over a bowl to drain milk solids. Rinse the block briefly, dry, and reserve.
Hollandaise: fill saucepot with 1 inch of water and bring to a gentle simmer.
Whisk 3 egg yolks in mixing bowl with 25 g water. Place bowl over simmering water.
Whisk in a figure-eight, rotating the bowl and removing from heat as needed for gentle, constant heat. About 2½ minutes total. Look for thickened, ribbon-consistency yolks with a pale yellow color.
Remove from heat. While whisking, add juice of half a lemon and slowly drizzle in warmed clarified butter. Add water as needed to maintain emulsion.
Season with additional lemon and salt to taste.
Plate: set 2 poached eggs on toast and spoon hollandaise to envelope each egg. Finish with black pepper and finishing salt.
recipes.notes: If sauce breaks: return to heat to fully break the yolks to curd, then add a little fresh yolk, warm it, and slowly drizzle the broken sauce back in. Break causes: too much heat, rushing, not enough water.

recipes.name: Béarnaise
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I

ingredients.name: shallots, peeled and sliced thin (for reduction)

instructions: Béarnaise reduction: place shallots, wine, vinegar, peppercorn, tarragon, and bay leaf in a saucepan. Reduce the liquids by one third. Remove bay leaf. Cool and reserve.
Béarnaise: place yolks, cream, and reduction in a 2-quart saucier; whisk over low heat until yolks expand to ribbon consistency.
Apply hollandaise technique — constant whisking, regulating heat to avoid scrambling.
Slowly drizzle in clarified butter, whisking to form an emulsion. Once incorporated, whisk in lemon juice, tarragon, shallots, and salt. Serve warm.
recipes.notes: For béarnaise mousseline: gently fold whipped cream into the béarnaise. For sauce choron: whisk ~50 g warmed tomato purée into ~500 g béarnaise. Classic pairings: béarnaise on eggs benedict; mousseline with steak and brussels sprouts.

recipes.name: Crème Anglaise (Vanilla)
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Combine milk, cream, and the scraped vanilla bean and pod in a saucepot over medium-low heat. Stir gently with rubber spatula and bring to a simmer.
Beat yolks until homogenous. Add sugar and a pinch of kosher salt; whisk to combine.
Temper: gradually ladle the hot milk/cream mixture into the yolks, whisking continuously. After ~4 ladles, the yolks reach the milk's temperature.
Whisk the tempered mixture back into the saucepot with the remaining vanilla cream.
Switch to a flat-bottom wooden spoon and stir as you cook to 185°F. Coat should be thick enough that a swipe across the back of the spoon remains.
Strain through a chinois into a mixing bowl set in an ice bath. Remove vanilla pod for another use. Whisk to cool to room temperature.
recipes.notes: If it curdles, recover by blending. Variations: chocolate (strain hot sauce over chocolate to melt); coffee (add grounds while cooking, then strain). Save the vanilla pod for vanilla sugar.

recipes.name: Swiss Meringue with Macerated Strawberries
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Macerated strawberries & coulis: add quartered strawberries to a bowl and mix in sugar (start at 25 g, add as needed). Place half the macerated berries and lemon juice in a beaker, blend with an immersion blender, strain the purée and reserve. Set aside the other half for garnish.
Meringue: combine egg whites, granulated sugar, and vanilla in a mixing bowl. Place over simmering water and whisk to 150°F.
Transfer to stand mixer bowl. Whip low → medium-high, then add sifted powdered sugar and whip on high.
Whip ~15 minutes until glossy with stiff peaks.
Arrange a silpat-lined sheet pan. Keep a quenelle spoon in the hot water — sticky meringue slides off cleanly. Form 6 quenelles.
Bake at 180°F for 45 minutes. Look for a crackly exterior crust and a soft, creamy interior.
Lightly torch the peaks to caramelize, dust with confectioners' sugar.
Plate with macerated strawberries, strawberry purée, whole strawberries, crème anglaise, and a pop of lime zest.
recipes.notes: Swiss meringue technique: gently beat whites + sugar over a bain-marie before whipping. Stable, silky, ideal for buttercream too.

recipes.name: Soft-Boiled Eggs
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Place eggs in a saucepot, cover with cold water by at least ½ inch, bring to a gentle boil.
Once boiling, lower heat to maintain the boil and start a 5-minute timer.
After 5 minutes, run cold water over the eggs until just cool enough to handle (peels easier while warm).
Peel in a cool water bath, removing the thin membrane under the shell.
Top with EVOO and finishing salt (fleur de sel or Maldon).
recipes.notes: Keller's daily morning ritual. Times vary with egg size, pot size, and burner — find your timing (try 4/5/6/7 min).

recipes.name: Scrambled Eggs (American & French Style)
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Both styles: crack each egg into a small bowl first to catch shell, then transfer to mixing bowl. Season with kosher salt. Whisk. For more refinement, blend then pass through a chinois.
American style: heat nonstick pan over very low heat. Add ~2 Tbsp (32 g) butter. Pour in eggs and gently scramble with rubber spatula as they set.
Remove pan before eggs are fully done — they continue cooking. Stir in 25 g crème fraîche and spoon onto a plate. Finish with parsley and Maldon.
French style (oeufs brouillés): set saucier over low heat. Add ~3 Tbsp (48 g) butter, pour in eggs. Whisk slowly and continuously to emulsify the butter and gently cook.
When eggs are semi-liquid but resemble porridge, turn off heat. Look for small curds pulling from the bottom and sides.
Whisk in ~½ Tbsp butter, 1 Tbsp crème fraîche, and parsley to taste. Spoon into a serving bowl, finish with Maldon, serve with brioche soldiers.
recipes.notes: Slow heat is essential to both. Refinement step (blend + chinois) elevates texture.

recipes.name: Poached Eggs
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Bring water and vinegar to a gentle simmer (taste for slightly acidic).
Crack each egg into its own small bowl.
Create a vortex by swirling vigorously around the edges of the pot. Slip an egg into the center; it sets into a teardrop shape.
Reinvigorate the vortex; add the next egg. Poach only 2–3 at a time.
After 2 minutes, gently lift with a slotted spoon and check yolk softness. Return if too soft.
Drain on paper towel; trim stringy whites with kitchen scissors. Serve on sliced brioche.
recipes.notes: Vinegar helps set the white. For batch poaching: poach ahead, ice bath, then reheat in simmering water 30–45 sec.

recipes.name: French Omelet
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Crack each egg into a small bowl, then transfer to a beaker. Blend with immersion blender and pass through a chinois.
Brush nonstick pan with beurre pommade; set over lowest heat. Pour in eggs.
When eggs start to set at the edges, transfer to a 250°F oven for 3–4 minutes — eggs begin to set and thicken but are not fully set.
Spread crème fraîche down the center, sprinkle with fines herbes and finishing salt.
Roll one edge to the center, continue rolling until you can slide the omelet seam-side down onto a plate.
Brush lightly with beurre pommade for sheen, finish with more fines herbes and Maldon.
recipes.notes: Mantra: slow, slow, slow. Beurre pommade is butter at mayonnaise-soft texture. Fillings to try: sautéed mushrooms, melted leeks, diced bacon (warmed first).

recipes.name: Fresh Egg Pasta Dough (Tipo 00)
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Mound flour on a pasta board. With a bench scraper, set aside about 1/6 of the flour (easier to add flour to wet dough than liquid to dry).
Make a large well. Pour in yolks, the whole egg, milk, olive oil, and salt.
With two fingers, swirl the ingredients, incorporating flour gradually until it becomes a thick paste.
Use the bench scraper to fold flour over the paste and cut it in. Knead until the dough is a smooth ball.
If sticky, add small amounts of reserved flour as needed.
Seal in plastic bag and refrigerate at least 4–5 hours (or overnight) to let gluten relax.
recipes.notes: Right consistency matters more than exact measurements — flour moisture and humidity vary. Italian grandmothers test the dough by feeling for the suppleness of their earlobe. Refrigerate at least 4–5 hours, or make a day ahead.

recipes.name: Pea & Mascarpone Agnolotti
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Pea farce: trim crusts from brioche, cube, process to fine crumbs.
Blanch peas in heavily salted water until soft, drain. Squeeze excess water in a lint-free towel while warm.
Process peas to smooth, add mascarpone and brioche crumbs, blend until homogeneous. Season with salt.
Pass farce through a tamis into a shallow container. Press plastic wrap on surface to prevent skin. Chill.
Pipe farce: insert 9/16-inch piping tip in bag, snip plastic to edge of tip, fill bag (don't overfill).

Shape agnolotti: cut a piece of dough slightly smaller than a stick of butter. Flatten to ~⅜ inch, run through pasta machine at widest setting. Fold in half and run through again, feeding folded edge first. Repeat 3–4 more times to develop a smooth texture.
Decrease pasta roller width to next setting, run dough through twice. Repeat, progressively reducing thickness, until the dough is very thin and translucent. Use as little flour as possible.
Lightly flour the pasta board. Lay dough sheet down. Pipe a bead of farce down the length of the center. Fold dough over the top.
Use your thumb to compress dough around the farce, then again to tighten. Pinch the bead between forefingers and thumbs to compress into ~⅝-inch wide pillows. Compress once more to seal.

With fluted pasta wheel, trim along the dough leaving ⅜ inch at the edge of the pillows. Starting from one end, with a quick decisive motion, roll through the middle of the pinched area between pillows to separate.
Inspect each agnolotti to ensure sealed edges; pinch as needed. Line up on an offset palette knife and transfer to a parchment-lined sheet pan in evenly spaced rows.
Refrigerate, or freeze on the tray and transfer to a sealed bag for storage.
recipes.notes: Work in small batches so dough doesn't dry. Piedmont-region pasta — pillows trap sauce in the rolled-over pocket. Pairs with the Agnolotti with Peas and Bacon finish (next recipe).

recipes.name: Agnolotti with Peas and Bacon
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Parmesan crisp: finely grate Parmesan. Heat nonstick pan over medium. Sprinkle Parmesan in even ⅛-inch layer across the bottom. Cook until golden and lacy. Remove with small offset palette knife and drape over a small cup while hot. Cool. (Can be made up to 1 hour ahead.)
Bring a stockpot of water to a simmer, season with salt.
Heat sauté pan over medium. Add chicken stock and a splash of water; simmer.
Add butter, season with salt and champagne vinegar (vinegar cuts the fat and elevates flavor).
Drop agnolotti in the pasta water; stir gently to prevent sticking. Cook until they float (time depends on size and whether frozen). Pasta finishes in the sauce.
Transfer floating agnolotti to the sauté pan with a skimmer. Swirl to coat. Adjust consistency with more stock if needed; add a little more butter to tighten the emulsion.
Add peas and bacon; cook until heated through.
Spoon into a serving dish and top with the Parmesan crisp.
recipes.notes: Single portion — stock/butter don't scale linearly for larger batches and may need a wider pan. Base technique applies to any flavor combo you'd build into a butter sauce.

recipes.name: Spaghetti alla Chitarra & Cavatelli (Shaping)
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Spaghetti alla chitarra: roll pasta sheet to slightly less than the thickness of a spaghetti noodle.
Trim sheet to fit over the chitarra strings. Allow the sheet to dry a few minutes — keeps strands separated.
Roll a rolling pin over the sheet to push it through the steel strings.
Spread noodles on a parchment-lined baking sheet to dry.
Cavatelli: roll dough into 1/16-inch sheet. Cut into ⅜-inch wide ribbons. Cut ribbons into 1-inch pieces.

Place each rectangle on the ridged side of a gnocchi paddle. With the edge of a butter knife, press the edge closest to you. Push down with your thumb and roll forward to curl the dough into the cavatelli shape (tightly rolled 'C').
recipes.notes: Two shaping techniques. Storage: dry pasta on sheet pan or as nests (keeps up to 1 month); or freeze on sheet pan and transfer to bag (up to 2 weeks).

recipes.name: Spaghetti Aglio e Olio (with Garlic Confit & Bottarga)
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Bring water to a simmer in a pasta pentola; lightly season with salt (water will form the sauce base — don't over-season).
Blanch dried pasta until it bends but is still very al dente.
Lift pasta to a 2-quart saucier with a strainer basket. Ladle enough pasta water to cover and bring to a simmer.
Spoon in garlic confit purée and stir with pasta fork to distribute. Continue cooking to glaze in the liquid to sauce consistency.
Taste for doneness — add more pasta water and cook longer if needed.
Add the whole confit garlic cloves and heat through. Drizzle in EVOO and sprinkle parsley.
Twist pasta on a fork into a serving dish. Spoon remaining garlic and sauce over. Finish with EVOO, lemon zest, and grated bottarga.
Without bottarga: garlic confit + lemon zest still finishes the dish beautifully.
recipes.notes: Uses dried spaghetti alla chitarra from the prior recipe and garlic confit from earlier in the workbook. Bottarga di muggine is salt-cured mullet roe — it brings a briny umami punch.

recipes.name: Potato Gnocchi
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Preheat oven to 350°F. Pierce potatoes with a fork. Pour a generous mound of salt on a baking sheet, set potatoes on top to stabilize.
Bake 1 hour, test with paring knife for done-ness. Soft and fully cooked. Brush off excess salt.
While potatoes are still hot, scoop flesh from jackets and push through a ricer onto a pasta board.
Form a well, sprinkle with flour. Add egg yolks, season with salt, sprinkle more flour. Use a bench scraper to mix.
Gently form a ball — do not knead (gluten → gummy gnocchi). Dough should be soft and hold a fingerprint.
With fingers (not palms), roll dough into a rope of your desired diameter. Cut into pieces and roll each into a ball.
Gently roll each ball on a gnocchi paddle to form ridged, ovular gnocchi; let pieces fall onto a sheet pan.
Season simmering water with salt. Test one gnocchi.
If it falls apart: more flour and a bit more working of the dough. If heavy/dense: note it for next batch.
Gnocchi float when done. Skim into an ice bath, drain on paper towels.
Serve immediately, refrigerate up to 2 days, or freeze on a lightly oiled parchment-lined sheet pan, then transfer to airtight freezer bag.
recipes.notes: Russet (starchy, floury) is best. Use potato flesh while still hot and moist. Italian-style gnocchi originates in Lombardy.

recipes.name: Gnocchi with Pomodoro Sauce
recipes.source: Thomas Keller MasterClass — Cooking Techniques I
instructions: Cut tomatoes in half on the equator, squeeze out seeds, and grate the seeded tomatoes on the fine side of a box grater into a bowl, leaving the skin behind (technique from Chef José Andrés).
Heat sauté pan over high heat. Add enough oil to barely coat the bottom.
When you see faint smoke, carefully add gnocchi and shake gently to prevent sticking. Let them lightly caramelize. Use the sloped edge of the pan to make them jump for even caramelization.
Season with salt. Remove pan from heat and grate in garlic. Return to heat and lightly sauté the garlic.
Add grated fresh tomatoes. Season with more salt and a bit of vinegar to taste (Parmesan will add salt later).
Remove from heat and top with torn basil. Spoon gnocchi and sauce onto a serving dish; finish with microplaned Parmesan.
recipes.notes: Pomodoro = fresh, quick sauce. Use canned San Marzanos when tomatoes are out of season. Pairs with frozen gnocchi without thawing.

recipes.name: Tuna Sashimi with Fennel Apple Salad

ingredients.name: Vietnamese rice paper rolls, broiled until crispy

instructions: Start with the avocado puree. Cut the avocado in quarters. Take out the pit and use a spoon to scrape out the contents. Pass it through a tamis, or blend it in a small blender. Squeeze in the lemon juice and season with salt.
Make the vinaigrette. Combine the chili paste and orange juice in a small bowl. Stir well. Season with salt.
Make the ponzu sauce. In another small bowl, add the soy sauce. Grate in ginger using a microplane. Squeeze in lemon juice. Mix together.

Salad: slice fennel bulb and apple on a mandolin. Julienne the slices and place in a bowl. Cut mesclun greens and add. Season with salt. Immediately dress with the ají chili vinaigrette to prevent browning.
Cut the tuna on an angle into pieces about 1/8 inch thick. Put 1/2 tsp ginger on each slice of tuna and roll up.

To plate: spread avocado puree across half the plate. Place 5 tuna pieces on the puree, drizzle ponzu. Pile salad in the center. Scatter radishes, jalapeños, daikon sprouts, edible flowers. Garnish by breaking pieces of broiled rice paper around the salad. Drizzle vinaigrette.
recipes.notes: Wolfgang suggests yellowtail, bigeye, or farm-raised bluefin as alternatives.

recipes.name: Veal Stock and Demi-Glace
instructions: Preheat oven to 500°F. Roast veal bones on a roasting pan for 45 min. Add celery, carrots, onions, garlic, peppercorns, thyme, rosemary, bay leaves; roast another 20 min.
Deglaze pan with red wine; add tomato paste. Transfer everything (including wine and pan scrapings) to stockpot.
Pressure cooker: add 4 qt water; lock and cook 1 hr 30 min, let sit 20 min.
Stockpot: add 4 qt water; simmer on low 5–6 hrs.
Demi-glace: strain stock into saucepot. Simmer uncovered over medium-high until reduced by half. Transfer to containers or ice cube trays.
recipes.notes: Yields ~2 qt stock, 1 qt demi-glace. Foundation for many sauces.

recipes.name: Pepper Steak with Red Wine Raisin Sauce
instructions: Combine raisins and red wine in a sauté pan over medium heat to plump the raisins.
Crush all peppercorns in a ziplock bag. Pour onto a plate.
Cut steaks (thicker for rare, thinner for well-done). Season both sides with salt; coat with crushed peppercorns.
Heat large sauté pan on high; add olive oil and bring to light smoke. Sear steaks 3–4 min per side. Rest on baking rack in warm oven.
Pan sauce: pour the wine-raisin mixture into the hot pan, reduce. Add demi-glace, whisk. Lower heat; add heavy cream, whisk and reduce until it coats the back of a spoon. Season with salt.
To plate: slice steak into 8 pieces, fan onto plate. Watercress alongside; drizzle with olive oil and spoon sauce over and around.
recipes.notes: Uses demi-glace from prior chapter.

recipes.name: Farro Salad with Roasted Carrots
instructions: Farro: combine water, farro, 2 tsp salt in a saucepan. Boil, then reduce and simmer covered 15–20 min until tender. Drain and cool in a bowl.
Carrots: preheat oven to 450°F. Heat olive oil in sauté pan, add shallot and garlic. Add carrots; squeeze lemon over. Toss. Roast 15–18 min. Cool, then halve or third.
Vinaigrette: in a bowl combine greek yogurt, shallot, blood orange peel, carrot tops (or mint). Add blood orange juice and lemon juice. Season; thin with more juice if needed. Pour into farro.
To plate: spoon farro down center. Top with roasted carrots, blood orange and orange segments, watercress, edible flowers, carrot ribbons.
recipes.notes: Highlights natural sweetness of carrots through heavy roasting.

recipes.name: Roasted Chicken with Mustard Port Sauce
instructions: Preheat oven to 500°F. Season chicken with salt and pepper. Heat sauté pan over medium-high, coat with olive oil. Sear chicken skin-side down 3–4 min.
When skin is golden, transfer pan to oven 8–12 min, until internal temp hits 165°F.
Back on stovetop, flip chicken. Add garlic and thyme. Baste until skin is golden and temp confirms 165°F. Rest on rack; remove thyme and garlic.
Sauce: deglaze pan with port wine. Reduce. Add veal demi-glace, whisk, reduce ~1 min. Off heat, whisk in whole grain and Dijon mustards. Season.
Salad: combine dandelion greens, broccolini, parsley. Drizzle lemon juice and olive oil. Toss; season.
Plate chicken skin-side up; sauce on top and around; salad alongside.
recipes.notes: Demi-glace from prior chapter. Substitute mushroom or garlic-butter sauce per Wolfgang's suggestion.

recipes.name: Béchamel Sauce, Mac & Cheese, and Creamed Spinach
instructions: Béchamel: melt butter in saucepot over medium. Add flour gradually, stir smooth; cook 2–3 min. Heat milk separately just below boil. Add hot milk to butter-flour 1/2 cup at a time, whisking constantly. Cook 12 min, stirring. Off heat, whisk in egg yolks one at a time. Season with salt and nutmeg.
Mac and Cheese: preheat oven to 500°F. Coat cooked macaroni with béchamel (don't drown). Add cheddar and mozzarella, toss. Season.
Transfer to cast iron skillet. Top with breadcrumbs and dots of butter. Bake 8–12 min until golden.
Creamed Spinach: sauté spinach in olive oil in batches until just wilted. Shock in ice bath, wring out, chop finely.
Warm béchamel; fold spinach in to taste, thinning with milk if needed. Season.
Fry eggs in butter; season. Place one on top of each portion of creamed spinach.
recipes.notes: Béchamel is one of the five French mother sauces; becomes Mornay when cheese is added.

recipes.name: Roasted Herb Branzino with Caper Herb Beurre Blanc
instructions: Herb crust: pulse breadcrumbs, parsley, rosemary, thyme, tarragon, chives in food processor until herbs are minced and breadcrumbs are green. Transfer to baking sheet.
Preheat oven to 550°F or broil. Oil a baking sheet. Brush fillets with olive oil, season. Press meat-side into the breadcrumbs to coat. Lay skin-side down; cook 5–8 min.

Beurre blanc: olive oil in sauté pan over medium. Sauté shallots until translucent. Deglaze with white wine; add tarragon. Reduce. Add lemon juice (thin with water if over-reduced). Whisk in butter gradually. Season. Add capers, tomatoes, parsley, lemon segments; whisk to combine.
Plate fillet skin-side down; spoon sauce around.
recipes.notes: Branzino is Mediterranean sea bass. Wolfgang loves tarragon for fish.

recipes.name: Oatmeal Risotto with Morels and Pea Puree

ingredients.name: snap peas, cut at a 45° angle

instructions: Vegetable stock: in stockpot over medium-high, sauté leek, carrots, celery in olive oil. Add thyme and cover with water. Simmer 1 hr. Strain through chinois. Keep hot.

Risotto: coat saucepot with olive oil over medium-high. Sauté shallots and garlic without browning. Add oats; coat in fat. Deglaze with white wine. Slowly add hot stock one ladle at a time, stirring constantly, until creamy with slight firmness. Season.
Pea puree: boil 4 cups salted water; add peas until they float. Blanch in ice water for color. Puree in blender (add blanching liquid as needed) until smooth.

Vegetables: quarter morels; submerge in water, lift out by hand to leave grit. Heat olive oil in sauté pan, add morels, salt, pepper, thyme, shallots, garlic. Cook until water evaporates. Add snap peas briefly to keep crunch. Season.
Fold a small amount of pea puree into the risotto just before serving for color. Freeze the rest.
Plate: scoop risotto into the center, shake to spread. Spoon morels in the center. Top with pea tendrils, mint, a squeeze of lemon, drizzle of olive oil.
recipes.notes: Vegan if no parmesan added. Wolfgang suggests sausage or chicken for non-vegetarians.

recipes.name: Seafood Gazpacho
instructions: Clam stock: in stockpot over medium-high, heat olive oil. Add vegetables and tarragon. Deglaze with ~2 cups white wine. Reduce by half, add washed clams, cover. Steam until clams open, 8–12 min. Strain juice through fine sieve over ice. Remove clams.
Tomato broth: in a bowl combine tomatoes, paprika, cayenne, sherry vinegar, olive oil, salt (can marinate overnight). Pass through food mill or blend and sieve. Add 2 cups clam juice; whisk. Taste.

Plate: arrange lobster pieces in the center of the bowl with cucumber slices. Pour ~1 cup soup. Place a shelled clam in the center. Garnish with cherry tomato slices, kumquats, gooseberries, grape slices, clam meat, diced celery, celery leaves. Squeeze lemon. Drizzle olive oil.
recipes.notes: Yields 6 cups. Oregano or thyme can substitute for tarragon.

recipes.name: Berry Margarita
instructions: In cocktail shaker, combine berries and lime rind. Mash to puree.
Add tequila, lime juice, simple syrup. Fill with ice. Shake.
Large ice cube in each glass. Strain in. Garnish with a skewer of berries and a lime twist.
recipes.notes: Use large ice cubes to avoid watering down. Substitute berries by season.

recipes.name: Negroni Cocktail
instructions: 3 large ice cubes in a pitcher.
Pour gin, vermouth, Campari; stir. Add champagne. Stir. Dash in Angostura and lemon bitters. Taste.
Strain into glasses. Garnish with lemon and lime twists.
recipes.notes: Italian aperitivo.

recipes.name: Bellini Cocktail
instructions: Pour peach puree into a pitcher with ice. Slowly pour in champagne, stir gently. Taste.
Strain into glasses; top with more sparkling wine if desired.
Peach puree: blanch peaches 15–20 sec, shock, peel. Halve, pit, chop. Combine with lemon juice and sugar; blend; pass through a fine sieve.
recipes.notes: Veneto-region summer cocktail.

recipes.name: Bloody Mary
instructions: Place tomatoes and jalapeño slices in a shaker. Salt and pepper. Add simple syrup, lemon juice, horseradish. Muddle.
Add vodka and ice. Shake.
Ice in glass; top with strained Bloody Mary. Garnish with celery stalk and a skewered lemon wedge + cherry tomato.
recipes.notes: Inspired by farmers' market tomatoes.

recipes.name: Grilled Steak and Broccolini
instructions: Build a charcoal fire and create different temperature zones: keep coals confined to one area of the grill, with a 'cool zone' on the other side (placing a log on the bottom and dumping coals next to it works well).
Drizzle a little grapeseed oil on the steak, then season generously with kosher salt well in advance of cooking so it can form a brine and tenderize the muscle.
Place steak directly over the coals to sear. Flip frequently and move around the grill according to how each side is responding; don't let one side cook unattended for too long.

If the exterior has a perfect sear but the interior is still spongy, move the steak off the coals into the cool zone to finish via indirect heat. (Or reverse-sear: cook over the cool zone first, then sear over coals at the end.)

Cook the broccolini on a grate over the coals in a chimney starter (concentrated heat in a small area). Keep the stems over the fire while the more delicate crowns sit unscathed; once the stems are tender, flip the broccolini around and quickly char the crowns.
Pull the steak at your target internal temperature (120°F rare, 130°F medium-rare, 140°F medium, 150°F medium-well, 160°F well done) using an instant-read thermometer.
Rest the steak a few minutes to reabsorb juices. Slice against the grain.
Season the slices once more with flaky sea salt before serving alongside the broccolini.
recipes.notes: Different temperature zones are the secret. Aaron recommends regular flipping rather than the 'sear-once' school. Maillard browning kicks in above 300°F exterior temp, while internal target for rare-to-medium is 120-140°F.

recipes.name: Smoked Pork Butt

ingredients.name: Yellow mustard or hot sauce, for slather
Water, beer, or apple cider vinegar, for spritzing

instructions: If the pork butt was sold with the skin on, remove it (the skin blocks smoke and rub). Don't bother trimming surface fat — the pork will be shredded.
Mix the rub: equal parts kosher salt and 16-mesh black pepper with a small amount of paprika for color. You'll need about 1/2 cup for an 8-10 lb butt.
Slather the non-presentation side with mustard or hot sauce, then sprinkle the rub in an even layer from side to side. Cup your hand along the sides to press rub onto them.
Flip butt fat side up. Slather and rub the presentation side. Let rest 30-40 minutes at room temp.
STAGE 1 (3 hrs): Get smoker to a consistent 270°F with clean smoke. Place pork butt fat cap up and cook undisturbed.

STAGE 2 (5 hrs): Spritz thoroughly with water, beer, or apple cider vinegar. Continue at 270°F for ~5 more hours, spritzing once per hour. Watch for the bark on the fat cap to split as the meat shrinks — that's the cue to wrap.

STAGE 3 (wrap, ~8 hr mark): Lay two overlapping wide sheets of aluminum foil shiny side up. Place pork fat side up about 8 inches from the bottom edge. Spritz once more, then spritz the foil. Tightly fold bottom over top, fold sides at obtuse angles, then roll the butt over to encase. Tuck excess foil and feel for air pockets.
STAGE 4 (2 hrs): Return wrapped butt to smoker. Cook 1 hour at 270°F, then raise to 295°F for 1 final hour.
STAGE 5: After ~10 hours total, internal temp should be just over 200°F. The meat should feel squishy and soft in your hands. Rest wrapped at room temp for 1 hour.
Carefully unwrap, saving the juices. Pour juices over the pork and shred with fingers or tongs. Discard or save the bone. Remove or chop in any big unrendered fat pockets. Serve.
recipes.notes: Bone-in gives more uniform shape. Pork butt is almost impossible to over-season since the bark will be torn apart and mixed with interior meat.

recipes.name: Smoked Pork Spare Ribs

ingredients.name: Rack of pork spare ribs, 3.5-4.5 pounds
Yellow mustard or hot sauce, for slather
16-mesh 'café grind' black pepper (2:1 pepper-to-salt for ribs)
Apple cider vinegar, for thinning sauce and spritzing

instructions: TRIM: Lay rack parallel to cutting board edge. Identify top (straight) and bottom (curved) edges, and presentation (outside) vs inside.

Remove the sternum and the thick cartilage behind it: cut it off at an angle, then clean the bottom edge with a thin slice along the length, leaving a smooth slightly-curved edge. Round off the far end so the rack has an aerodynamic shape.
Trim the skirt (diagonal flap on the inside) if still attached. Silverskin is optional — Aaron leaves it. Feel around and remove any stray bone bits or excess fat.
RUB: Mix kosher salt and black pepper at a 2:1 ratio (pepper-heavy for ribs) with a small amount of paprika. You'll need ~1/4 cup per rack.

Slather the inside with mustard or hot sauce, then sprinkle rub from side to side parallel to the bones. Flip and repeat on the presentation side. Go a little heavier with slather and rub on the fattier portions. Let rest at room temp while building the fire.

STAGE 1 (3 hrs): Get smoker to consistent 265-270°F with clean smoke. Place ribs in chamber with the thickest part closest to the fire. Spritz edges with water, beer, or apple cider vinegar at the end of hours 1 and 2 as needed.

STAGE 2 (sauce, ~2.5 hrs in): Mix equal parts warm rib sauce and apple cider vinegar in a squeeze bottle. Spritz the rack thoroughly. Squeeze the diluted sauce on top in an even layer parallel to the bones; work it around with your hand until the entire presentation side is coated. Light spritz again, close lid for ~10 min. Flip and sauce the other side, then close for another 10 min.

STAGE 3 (wrap): Remove rack by hand (not tongs). Pull out any emerging bone chunks so they don't puncture the foil. Cut a sheet of wide foil twice as long as the rack, shiny side up. Spritz foil and spread a little more sauce on it; lay ribs presentation side DOWN on the sauce about 3 inches from the bottom edge. Spritz the top.

Wrap: fold both ends over so they overlap in the center. Tuck the foil tight around the bottom edge to conform. Fold over each diagonal corner where the sternum was, then tuck along the top. Fold the top edge over and fold both sides in tightly at obtuse angles.
STAGE 4 (3 hrs): Return wrapped ribs to smoker with seam facing up; cook 3 more hours at 265-270°F.
STAGE 5: Remove and let rest in foil, seam up, for 30-40 minutes. Feel around the sternum for the third rib bone — soft and pliable means done.

SERVE: Unwrap, careful not to spill juices. With bottom of ribs facing away, lift the far end of foil and flip the ribs toward you onto the cutting board, presentation side up with juices pouring over. Slice between each bone.
recipes.notes: Aaron does a '3-3' cook (3 hrs on, 3 hrs wrapped) rather than the classic '3-2-1'. The diluted sauce reduces sugar that would otherwise burn in the smoker. If the fat looks like it's rendering before you wrap, reduce smoker temp — render should happen after wrapping so it emulsifies with the sauce. See 'Aaron's Rib Sauce' recipe.

recipes.name: Aaron's Rib Sauce

ingredients.name: Fat (beef tallow, vegetable oil, lard, or bacon fat)
Large yellow or white onion, roughly chopped

instructions: Heat a saucepan over medium heat and add the fat. Once it shimmers, add the onion and cook until soft and translucent, 6-8 minutes. Add the garlic and continue cooking until the onion has browned and the garlic has started turning crisp, about 3 minutes more.
Add the brown sugar and cook, stirring frequently, until the sugar melts and starts to form a glaze, 2-3 minutes.

Stir in apple cider vinegar, ketchup, smoked paprika, mustard powder, salt, and pepper. Bring to a simmer and cook 3-5 minutes until thickened slightly. Add 4 dashes of Worcestershire and simmer 1 more minute.
Transfer to a blender and blend at high speed until smooth and orange-hued, about 1 minute. Pulse once or twice before going to full blend (hot liquids splatter).
Transfer to a heat-resistant container and cool to room temperature. Store refrigerated up to 1 month.
recipes.notes: Worcestershire is measured in dashes (4 dashes). Aaron prefers organic/all-natural ketchup without high-fructose corn syrup — lower sugar content makes the sauce less likely to burn in the smoker.

recipes.name: Smoked Texas-Style Brisket

ingredients.name: Yellow mustard, hot sauce, or water, for slather
Water, beer, or apple cider vinegar, for spritzing

instructions: TRIM (cold from fridge): Use a stiff 8-inch boning knife. Remove ~1/2 inch from each long edge (rough/discolored split side) with long smooth strokes to expose the flat. Trim the thin end of the flat if needed so it survives the long cook.

Lay brisket fat-cap up. Find the dimples where the cap likely ends. Slice into the fat at a curved angle, peeling back the top waxy layer with your other hand. Shave upper layers until a pillowy ~1/4-inch layer of soft white fat remains. Trim some hardened fat from the side of the point. Leave the thick seam-fat pocket under the point in place for now.
Flip fat-down. Slice off the exposed seam fat at the flat/point junction. Remove the deckle if present (thick hard fat that connected to the rib cage), any silverskin, and stray bits of muscle.
RUB: Mix equal parts kosher salt and 16-mesh black pepper (~1/2 cup total for a 12 lb brisket). Optionally go a little salt-heavier on the point and pepper-heavier on the flat.

Slather meat side (fat down) lightly with mustard, hot sauce, or water — just enough to be tacky. Shake rub across in even side-to-side layers; avoid filling deep pockets. Gently pat in. Cup hand along each edge and pour rub directly into your hand as you move along, pressing onto the side.
Flip fat side up, slather and rub. Pat in. Let brisket rest at room temp 30-40 minutes.
STAGE 1 (3 hrs): Bring smoker to a steady 255°F with clean, bluish smoke. Place brisket point closest to fire, lid closed, undisturbed. This sets the flavor base.
STAGE 2 (3 hrs): Open and check. Should be mahogany with consistent bark. Spritz dryer/vulnerable edges. Raise temp to 260-265°F. Cook 3 more hours, checking and spritzing once per hour.

STAGE 3 (stall, ~hr 6, ~1 hr): At ~165°F internal the brisket hits the stall (evaporative cooling). Ramp temp to 280-285°F to push through. After ~1 hour, lift the brisket — if it bends at the edges, you're through the stall.

STAGE 4 (wrap): The flat is your barometer — when it's firm but a little floppy at the edge, and the bark is starting to crack, it's ready. Lay two overlapping wide sheets of butcher paper (preferred) or foil, four times as long as the brisket is wide. Place brisket presentation side up, ~1 foot from bottom edge. Spritz brisket and the paper. Wrap: fold bottom edge over the top tightly, conforming to the shape. Fold one side tightly across the flat at an obtuse angle. Tuck the opposite side under the point, then fold over the top. Roll brisket over once, fold sides again. Fold top end over to double thickness, then roll brisket one more time so presentation side is up with double layer beneath.

STAGE 5 (~3-4 hrs): Return wrapped brisket to smoker, point closest to fire. Smoke quality no longer matters — focus on temp. Cook undisturbed at 275-285°F for ~3 hours, then gradually let temp taper off for the final hour.
STAGE 6: Check tenderness with hands (use a towel) every ~15 minutes. When the brisket feels loose, soft, and a bit jiggly, pull it. Better too soon than too late.
REST in the wrap until internal temp drops to 140-150°F — at least 30 min, up to 1-2 hours. Carryover cooking continues.

SLICE just before serving with a long-bladed knife (Aaron uses a 12-inch serrated bread knife). Slice the FLAT first against the grain, starting opposite the point, pencil-width slices, gradually tapering thickness.

For the POINT: cut off and discard the thick seam-fat pocket beneath one side. Slice the point in half lengthwise (the 'money shot'). Slice ~3/8-inch thick across the grain, tapering on the side closest to you. Trim the second seam-fat pocket from the other half. Reserve the final flat piece and the ridge ('burnt ends'): chop the flat piece for beans or chopped beef, and cut the ridge into bite-size burnt-end snacks.
recipes.notes: Look for prime > choice > select grading and good marbling. A thick hard fat cap can signal industrial raising. Trim cold; rub at room temp; smoke at 255°F → 260-265°F → 280-285°F. Butcher paper > foil for breathability and bark. Aaron's preferred slicing knife is an inexpensive 12-inch serrated bread knife.
